blocks.text: FOI laws are among the most important instruments of democratic governance. They grant citizens, journalists, researchers, and civil society organisations the legal right to access information held by public authorities, enabling public scrutiny, informed participation, and government accountability.

Over the past three decades, FOI laws have spread rapidly around the world and are now recognised as a cornerstone of open government. Yet, despite their widespread adoption, many public administrations fail to provide the level of transparency promised by legislation. Requests may receive incomplete responses, be refused without adequate justification, or simply go unanswered. This persistent gap between the legal right to information and its practical implementation remains a major challenge for contemporary democracies.

TRANSACT seeks to explain why this implementation gap exists and under which conditions Freedom of Information laws effectively promote transparency. By combining implementation audits, observational studies, and randomised field experiments, the project investigates how interactions between citizens and public administrations shape transparency outcomes across different institutional contexts.
A Practice-Based Perspective on Transparency
TRANSACT approaches the implementation of Freedom of Information laws as an everyday administrative practice shaped by interactions between citizens and public officials.

The project examines how the characteristics of information requests, the exercise of bureaucratic discretion, and broader institutional and societal conditions influence whether public authorities disclose information. This perspective helps explain why similar legal provisions may produce different transparency outcomes across administrations and countries.
Drawing on insights from public policy, public administration, and organisational research, TRANSACT seeks to advance a comparative understanding of the mechanisms shaping FOI implementation.
Research Methodology

TRANSACT combines three complementary empirical approaches to investigate how Freedom of Information laws are implemented in practice. By integrating implementation audits, observational studies, and randomised field experiments, the project examines whether public authorities comply with transparency obligations, how FOI systems operate in everyday practice, and which factors explain differences in administrative responsiveness.
Implementation Audits
TRANSACT conducts systematic audits of FOI implementation by submitting standardised information requests to public authorities and assessing their responses against applicable legal requirements.

These studies measure administrative responsiveness, response times, information disclosure, and compliance with statutory obligations. They provide evidence of the gap between legally guaranteed access to information and actual administrative performance.
Observational Studies Using FOI Platform Data
TRANSACT analyses large-scale datasets of real information requests submitted through digital FOI platforms, including Transparencia.be and AskTheEU.

Using computational social science techniques, including natural language processing and large language models, the project investigates patterns of FOI use, requester behaviour, administrative responsiveness, disclosure outcomes, and changes over time.
These analyses provide insights into how citizens and public authorities interact through FOI mechanisms in real-world settings.
Randomised Field Experiments

TRANSACT conducts randomised field experiments in which standardised FOI requests are submitted to public authorities while systematically varying selected characteristics, such as requester identity, references to FOI legislation, and request framing.
Random assignment enables researchers to identify the causal effects of these characteristics on administrative responsiveness, response times, and information disclosure.
An Integrated Research Approach

The three methodologies provide complementary perspectives on FOI implementation. Implementation audits assess compliance with legal obligations, observational studies reveal patterns of FOI use and administrative behaviour, and field experiments identify the causal mechanisms influencing bureaucratic responsiveness.

Together, these approaches allow TRANSACT to document the implementation gap, investigate how transparency operates in everyday administrative practice, and explain the conditions under which Freedom of Information laws effectively deliver access to public information.
